text_original: UNESCO records that Kimjang follows a yearly cycle: in spring households procure shrimp, anchovy and other seafood for salting and fermenting, in summer they buy sea salt for brine, in late summer red chilli peppers are dried and ground, and late autumn is Kimjang season, when communities make and share large quantities of kimchi so every household can last through winter.
text_en: According to UNESCO, kimjang follows a yearly cycle - seafood for fermenting in spring, sea salt in summer, dried and ground red chilli in late summer - culminating in late-autumn communal kimchi-making and sharing so each household has enough for winter.

source.title: Kimjang, making and sharing kimchi in the Republic of Korea

text_original: UNESCO describes kimchi as preserved vegetables seasoned with spices and fermented seafood that forms an essential part of Korean meals, transcending class and regional differences.
text_en: UNESCO says kimchi (vegetables preserved with spices and fermented seafood) is an essential part of Korean meals across classes and regions.

source.title: Kimjang, making and sharing kimchi in the Republic of Korea

text_original: According to UNESCO, kimjang methods and ingredients differ by region and are treated as an important family heritage, typically passed from a mother-in-law to her newly married daughter-in-law, and housewives monitor weather forecasts to choose the best date and temperature for making kimchi.
text_en: UNESCO notes regional differences in kimjang methods, transmission of family recipes from mother-in-law to daughter-in-law, and housewives' use of weather forecasts to time kimchi-making.

source.title: Kimjang, making and sharing kimchi in the Republic of Korea

text_original: In the Republic of Korea's part of the UNESCO listing, ssireum is wrestling in which two players wearing long fabric belts around the waist and one thigh grip each other's belt and use techniques to bring the opponent to the ground; the winner of the adult final receives an ox, symbolizing agricultural abundance, and the title 'Jangsa', and parades around the neighbourhood riding the ox.
text_en: In South Korea's ssireum, players grip belts on the waist and one thigh; the adult-final winner gets an ox (a symbol of agricultural abundance) and the title Jangsa, then parades through the neighbourhood riding it (UNESCO).

text_original: According to UNESCO, ssireum matches are held on sand in any available space in a neighbourhood, are open to community members of all ages from children to seniors, and are played on traditional holidays, market days and festivals.

text_original: 문화체육관광부 어린이 누리집은 윷놀이를 4개의 윷가락을 던져 나온 끗수(도·개·걸·윷·모)에 따라 29밭 말판 위에서 4개의 말을 이동시켜 먼저 빠져나오는 편이 이기는 민속놀이로 설명하며, 백제 시대에 이미 행해진 것으로 보이고 윷판은 북두칠성이 북극성을 중심으로 도는 모습을 본떴다고 한다.
text_en: MCST's children's site describes yutnori as a folk game where four sticks give scores (do, gae, geol, yut, mo) for moving four pieces around a 29-point board, apparently played since the Baekje period, its board said to mimic the Big Dipper circling the Pole Star.

source.title: 전통놀이 - 윷놀이

text_original: 윷놀이는 두 명 이상이 편을 나누어 윷가락을 던져 순서를 정하고, 자기편 말이 상대편 말이 있는 곳에 도달하면 상대 말을 잡고 윷을 한 번 더 던지며, 네 개의 말이 윷판을 돌아 참먹이로 먼저 빠져나오는 편이 이긴다.
text_en: In yutnori, two or more players form teams and throw sticks to set order; landing on an opponent's piece captures it and earns another throw, and the team that first brings all four pieces around the board to the last point (chammeogi) wins.

source.title: 전통놀이 - 윷놀이

text_original: UNESCO records that the four-week Gangneung Danoje Festival begins with the brewing of a sacred liquor and Dano shamanistic rituals centred on a sacred tree, the sinmok, and the hwagae, a ritual object of feathers, bells and bamboo wood.
text_en: The Gangneung Danoje Festival (Gangwon) lasts four weeks and opens with sacred-liquor brewing and shamanistic rituals using the sinmok tree and the hwagae ritual object (UNESCO).

source.title: Gangneung Danoje festival

text_original: According to UNESCO, the Gangneung Danoje Festival includes a shamanistic ritual on the Daegwallyeong Ridge honouring a mountain deity and tutelary deities, Odokddegi folk songs and the Gwanno mask drama, and features the coexistence of Confucian, shamanistic and Buddhist rituals.
text_en: Gangneung Danoje includes a mountain-deity ritual at Daegwallyeong Ridge, Odokddegi songs, Gwanno mask drama, and Confucian, shamanistic and Buddhist rituals side by side (UNESCO).

source.title: Gangneung Danoje festival

text_original: UNESCO describes the Nanjang market, Korea's largest outdoor marketplace, as a major element of the Gangneung Danoje Festival, and notes that visitors make festival fans, help brew the sacred liquor, draw masks for the Gwanno Mask Drama, prepare and eat Surichiwi rice crackers and wash their hair in iris water.
text_en: At Gangneung Danoje, the Nanjang open-air market is a major element, and visitors join in fan-making, liquor-brewing, mask-drawing, eating Surichiwi rice crackers and washing hair in iris water (UNESCO).

source.title: Gangneung Danoje festival

text_original: UNESCO describes Ganggangsullae as a seasonal harvest and fertility ritual popular in south-western Korea, performed primarily on Chuseok in the eighth lunar month, when dozens of young unmarried village women join hands in a circle under the full moon, and sing and dance all night led by a lead singer, miming scenes from farm and fishing village life.
text_en: Ganggangsullae, popular in south-western Korea, is a Chuseok harvest and fertility ritual in which unmarried village women circle-dance and sing all night under the full moon, miming farm and fishing scenes (UNESCO).

source.title: Ganggangsullae

text_original: VisitKorea states that the Seollal holiday lasts three consecutive days, with the main day between two additional public holidays, giving many Koreans the chance to return to their hometowns; customs include charye (ancestral rite), sebae (deep bow to elders), sharing tteokguk, and folk games such as yunnori and neolttwigi.
text_en: Seollal is a three-day holiday when many return to hometowns for charye, sebae, tteokguk and folk games like yunnori and neolttwigi (Korea Tourism Organization).

source.title: Three Major Traditional Korean Holidays: Seollal, Dano, and Chuseok (updated 2026-02-05)

text_original: VisitKorea says Dano originated from early-summer rituals of agricultural communities praying for a plentiful harvest, with customs including eating wheel-shaped rice cake, women washing their hair in water boiled with changpo (sweet flag), and men demonstrating strength through ssireum.
text_en: Dano began as an early-summer harvest ritual; customs include wheel-shaped rice cake, changpo hair washing for women and ssireum for men (Korea Tourism Organization).

source.title: Three Major Traditional Korean Holidays: Seollal, Dano, and Chuseok (updated 2026-02-05)

text_original: According to VisitKorea, on Chuseok families gather in the morning to honour ancestors with food offerings, then visit the ancestral grave and make wishes under the full moon; representative foods include songpyeon, japchae, namul, jeon and fresh fruit such as apples and pears, and the holiday period spans three consecutive days.
text_en: On Chuseok, families offer food to ancestors, visit graves and wish on the full moon; typical foods are songpyeon, japchae, namul, jeon and fruit; the holiday runs three days (Korea Tourism Organization).

source.title: Three Major Traditional Korean Holidays: Seollal, Dano, and Chuseok (updated 2026-02-05)

text_original: VisitKorea reports that in December 2023 the National Heritage Service designated five major traditional holiday observances - Seollal and Daeboreum (as one), Hansik, Dano, Chuseok and Dongji - as National Intangible Cultural Heritage.
text_en: In December 2023 Korea's National Heritage Service designated Seollal/Daeboreum, Hansik, Dano, Chuseok and Dongji as National Intangible Cultural Heritage (Korea Tourism Organization).

source.title: Three Major Traditional Korean Holidays: Seollal, Dano, and Chuseok (updated 2026-02-05)

text_en: In the 2025 Social Survey, 70.2% had travelled domestically, 31.5% had travelled abroad and 57.7% had attended arts or sports events in person in the past year, all higher than two years earlier.

text_en: In the 2025 Social Survey, 48.7% of people aged 13+ read a book, but the average number of books read fell compared with two years earlier.

text_original: UNESCO records that as the eighth day of the fourth lunar month (Buddha's birthday) approaches, the whole country lights up with colourful lanterns, the festival begins with bathing an image of the baby Buddha, and members of the public can take part by carrying lanterns they have made.
text_en: Yeondeunghoe lights colourful lanterns nationwide around Buddha's birthday (8th day of the 4th lunar month), starting with bathing a baby Buddha image, and the public can carry lanterns they have made (UNESCO).

source.title: Yeondeunghoe, lantern lighting festival in the Republic of Korea

text_original: UNESCO's Talchum account says an ensemble of six to ten musicians accompanies masked performers, that performances do not require a formal stage, and that Talchum dramas are an important part of local festivals.
text_en: Talchum mask dance dramas are performed without a formal stage to an ensemble of six to ten musicians and feature in local festivals (UNESCO account via Korea's UNESCO delegation).

source.title: Talchum, mask dance drama in the Republic of Korea (UNESCO, 2022)
source.publisher: Permanent Delegation of the Republic of Korea to UNESCO (MOFA)

text_original: UNESCO states that Jultagi performances feature some forty different rope techniques and can last several hours, that troupes are frequently invited to local festivals particularly in spring and autumn, and that transmission is centred on the Jultagi Safeguarding Association in Gyeonggi Province.
text_en: Jultagi tightrope performances use about forty rope techniques, are staged at local festivals mainly in spring and autumn, and are transmitted through the Jultagi Safeguarding Association in Gyeonggi (UNESCO).

source.title: Jultagi, tightrope walking

text_original: UNESCO records that Jeju Chilmeoridang Yeongdeunggut is held in the second lunar month to pray for calm seas, an abundant harvest and a plentiful sea catch, is primarily supported by female divers and ship owners, and includes the launching of a straw boat into the sea by the village's senior men.
text_en: On Jeju, the Chilmeoridang Yeongdeunggut rite in the second lunar month is supported mainly by female divers and ship owners, prays for calm seas and good catches, and ends with launching a straw boat (UNESCO).

source.title: Jeju Chilmeoridang Yeongdeunggut

text_original: UNESCO says pansori is performed by a vocalist and a drummer, that performances can last up to eight hours, that it originated in south-west Korea in the seventeenth century, and that it was designated a National Intangible Cultural Property in 1964.
text_en: Pansori is an epic chant by one vocalist and a drummer, lasting up to eight hours, originating in south-west Korea in the 17th century and designated a national intangible property in 1964 (UNESCO).

source.title: Pansori epic chant

text_original: UNESCO notes that Arirang has some 3,600 variations belonging to about sixty versions, and that everyone can create new lyrics to the refrain 'Arirang, arirang, arariyo'.
text_en: Arirang exists in roughly 3,600 variations (about sixty versions) and anyone can compose new lyrics to its refrain (UNESCO).

source.title: Arirang, lyrical folk song in the Republic of Korea

text_original: UNESCO describes nongak as community band music, dance and rituals performed to pray for a rich harvest in spring, celebrate it at autumn festivals and raise funds for community projects, with distinctive regional styles generally divided among five cultural centres.
text_en: Nongak is farmers' community band music, dance and ritual used to pray for harvest in spring, celebrate in autumn and raise community funds, with regional styles grouped into five cultural centres (UNESCO).

source.title: Nongak, community band music, dance and rituals in the Republic of Korea

text_original: Ministry of Employment and Labor figures reported by the Korea Herald show average monthly working hours of employees at 156.2 in 2023 (about 1,874 hours a year), down from 172.6 in 2013 (2,071.2 hours a year); annual hours first fell below 2,000 in 2017.
text_en: Korean employees averaged 156.2 monthly hours in 2023 (1,874 a year) versus 172.6 (2,071.2) in 2013.

source.title: South Koreans working 200 hours fewer than decade ago: Data (Korea Herald, 2024-03-04)

text_original: According to OECD data reported by the Korea Times, South Korea's average annual working hours were 1,833 in 2025, down from 1,865 in 2024 and 97 hours above the OECD average of 1,736, ranking sixth of 36 countries.
text_en: OECD data show Koreans averaged 1,833 working hours in 2025, 97 more than the OECD average, sixth-highest among 36 countries.

source.title: S. Korea's yearly working hours fall by 32 hours last year but remain longer than OECD average (2026-07-05)

text_original: The 52-hour workweek system, capping regular hours at 40 plus up to 12 hours of overtime, was introduced in July 2018 for firms with 300 or more employees and expanded to firms with 50-299 employees in January 2020.
text_en: South Korea's 52-hour workweek (40 regular + 12 overtime) began July 2018 for large firms and reached firms with 50-299 workers in January 2020.

source.title: Daily working hours dip slightly in 2024 under 52-hour workweek system

text_original: Statistics Korea's 2024 time-use survey found wage earners worked 6 hours 8 minutes a day on average (6:23 in 2019), men 6:36, one hour four minutes longer than women, and average sleep fell to 8 hours 4 minutes, the first decline since 1999.
text_en: In 2024 Korean wage earners worked 6h08m daily; men worked 1h04m more than women; average sleep dropped to 8h04m.

source.title: Daily working hours dip slightly in 2024 under 52-hour workweek system

text_original: UNESCO records that Jeju haenyeo dive about 10 m without oxygen masks to gather shellfish such as abalone or sea urchins for a living, harvest up to seven hours a day on about 90 days a year, hold their breath about one minute per dive, and are grouped by experience as hagun, junggun and sanggun, with sanggun guiding the others.
text_en: Jeju haenyeo dive ~10 m without oxygen masks, work up to seven hours a day on ~90 days a year, and are ranked hagun, junggun and sanggun, with sanggun guiding the rest (UNESCO).

source.title: Culture of Jeju Haenyeo (women divers)

text_original: According to UNESCO, haenyeo knowledge is passed to younger generations in families, schools, local fishery cooperatives holding the area's fishing rights, haenyeo associations, the Haenyeo School and the Haenyeo Museum.
text_en: Jeju haenyeo skills are transmitted through families, schools, fishery cooperatives (which hold fishing rights), associations, the Haenyeo School and Haenyeo Museum (UNESCO).

source.title: Culture of Jeju Haenyeo (women divers)

text_original: UNESCO records that weaving of mosi (fine ramie) in Hansan, South Chungcheong, is transmitted by middle-aged women; the process includes harvesting, boiling and bleaching ramie, spinning yarn from the fibre and weaving on a traditional loom, and the cloth is used for summer clothing including mourning garments.
text_en: In Hansan (South Chungcheong) middle-aged women weave mosi ramie cloth: harvesting, boiling, bleaching, spinning and loom weaving; it is used for summer clothes including mourning garments (UNESCO).

source.title: Weaving of Mosi (fine ramie) in the Hansan region

text_original: According to UNESCO, mosi weaving traditionally takes place in women-led family operations in which mothers pass techniques to daughters or daughters-in-law, neighbours work together in a designated section of town, and around 500 people in the province were engaged in fine-ramie weaving.
text_en: Hansan mosi weaving is a women-led family craft passed from mothers to daughters or daughters-in-law, with neighbours working together; about 500 people in the province were involved (UNESCO).

source.title: Weaving of Mosi (fine ramie) in the Hansan region
